title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident shows AI being used as a tool for impersonation and fabrication outside any single deployed system. Scammers generated deepfake images and videos of named public figures, and produced fake news articles depicting interviews that never occurred, in order to lend false credibility to an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The failure is not a malfunction of a legitimate AI product but the deliberate use of AI capabilities, specifically synthetic media generation, to deceive consumers about the endorsement and legitimacy of a fraudulent investment scheme.

The deception operated across multiple layers, combining fabricated articles, fake websites, and bogus reviews into a coordinated structure. This layering means no single content check at any one platform would have caught the full scheme. Catching it earlier would have required coordinated detection across the hosting platforms carrying the fake articles, the social platforms distributing the deepfake videos, and the financial services registers that could flag the unlicensed entity being promoted.

What is not established is the identity of those responsible, and the ASIC warning and associated reporting constitute regulatory concern and observed data, not findings of guilt against any specific individual or organisation.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article falsely depicted Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler, where she supposedly objected to questions about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article never actually happened but exemplifies a rising scam trend that ASIC says is becoming increasingly sophisticated thanks to artificial intelligence. Scammers are creating fake deepfake images and videos of well-known Australians, including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Gina Rinehart, and Alan Kohler himself, to promote fraudulent investment schemes.

According to new ASIC research released today, investment scams have exploded in prevalence and complexity. Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams, up 182 percent, including 5,476 phishing scams and 7,051 fake investment platforms. Scammers build elaborate webs of deception using fabricated news articles, fake websites, and bogus reviews to lure victims who provide personal details and eventually money. ASIC urges consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers, while Kohler argues that platforms hosting such content should face heavy fines.
